questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from the poem "Blood" where the outcome contradicts the character's intention or expectation.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is sharply contrary to what was expected or intended. In "Blood," the speaker promises her great-grandmother as a child: "When I grow old... I shall rebuild the fallen walls / And make new this ancient house." The situational irony is that she grows old but never rebuilds; instead, she leaves the house to decay and watches it burn at her grandmother's cremation. A wrong answer that cites the grandmother's pride in "oldest blood" while living in a crumbling house identifies dramatic irony (contrast between character's belief and reality known to reader), not situational irony (contrast between intention and outcome).

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the ancestral house functions as a symbol in the poem. What abstract idea does it represent, and how does its physical description reinforce that meaning?
questions.a: The ancestral house symbolizes the fading aristocratic tradition and the weight of inherited identity. Its physical decay — "walls are cracked and torn," "tiles have fallen," "rats come out," "snake-shrine is dark with weeds" — mirrors the erosion of the feudal order and the great-grandmother's compromised life. The house "crouching on its elbows" and later appearing "grotesque and alive" in the moonlight personifies tradition as a dying, almost sentient entity. A wrong answer that says the house merely represents "the past" or "memory" misses the specific critique: the house embodies a tradition built on privilege ("oldest blood") that the poet both inherits and rejects, making it a symbol of complicity as much as heritage.

questions.q: Identify one instance of verbal irony in the poem where the speaker says something but means the opposite, or where the literal meaning undermines the speaker's stated feeling. Quote the lines and explain the irony.
questions.a: The lines "Call me callous / Call me selfish / But do not blame my blood / So thin, so clear, so fine" contain verbal irony. The speaker invites condemnation ("callous," "selfish") to deflect it from her bloodline, but the very act of defending her "oldest blood" while abandoning the house that blood built reveals the hollowness of aristocratic pride. The irony deepens because she claims the blood "remembers as it flows / All the gems and all the gold" — yet she has forgotten her promise. A wrong answer that points to the great-grandmother saying "O it hurts me she cried / For I love this house" misses verbal irony; that is sincere emotion, not a contradiction between words and meaning.

questions.q: Compare the symbolism of "blood" in the great-grandmother's worldview versus the poet's adult perspective. How does the same symbol shift in meaning across the poem?
questions.a: For the great-grandmother, "blood" symbolizes pure aristocratic lineage — "thin and clear and fine," distinct from the "thick as gruel / And muddy as a ditch" blood of the poor and new-rich. It legitimizes her past grandeur (elephant rides, jewel boxes, prince husband). For the adult poet, "blood" becomes an ironic symbol of inescapable inheritance she cannot honor: she invokes its purity ("do not blame my blood") while acknowledging she has "let you down / Old house." The symbol shifts from badge of honor to burden of guilt. A wrong answer that treats "blood" as a static symbol of family heritage misses the poem's central tension: the poet uses the grandmother's own symbol to justify her betrayal, exposing the symbol's fragility.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the poem's ending — the speaker hearing the house's "rattle of its death" from "every town I live in" — resolves or intensifies the irony of her broken promise. Justify your judgment with evidence.
questions.a: The ending intensifies the irony rather than resolving it. The speaker has physically escaped ("I set forth again / For other towns"), but the house haunts her psychologically: "From every town I live in / I hear the rattle of its death." The irony is that her mobility — enabled by the very modernity that doomed the house — cannot free her from its auditory ghost. The house's "windows close / Like the closing of the eyes" and "pillars groan" mirror her grandmother's death, suggesting the speaker has internalized the house's demise. A wrong answer claiming the ending brings closure ("she asks forgiveness") confuses the speaker's performative apology ("I seek forgiveness") with genuine resolution; the persistent haunting proves the irony endures.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza that uses situational irony and a central symbol to depict a modern Indian teenager's relationship with a family tradition (e.g., festival ritual, language, craft). The irony must arise from a gap between intention and outcome.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) establish a clear tradition (e.g., grandmother teaching rangoli), (2) state the teenager's sincere intention to preserve it ("I swore I'd learn every design"), (3) show the ironic outcome (she becomes a graphic designer but never draws rangoli again), and (4) use a symbol (the rice flour / the design app on her screen) that embodies the tradition's transformation. Example: "I swore I'd learn each rice-flour line / That grandmother drew at dawn / Now pixels glow on my design screen — / The rangoli lives, but the hand is gone." A weak answer describes the tradition without irony (e.g., "I love making rangoli with grandma") or uses only verbal irony (saying "I hate rangoli" while making it), missing the situational gap between youthful vow and adult reality.
